en: A state of temporary suspension or inactivity
hook: ABEYANCE: 'A BAY' where ships wait, temporarily paused.
story: Abeyance. The government announced a new metro line through Shuvo's neighbourhood, and construction began. Then a court case was filed over land rights. Work stopped, the cranes stood idle, and the project was held in abeyance: a state of temporary suspension. It was not cancelled, only paused until the court decided. Things in abeyance can be revived later. Picture a ship waiting at anchor in a bay, going nowhere for now. Synonyms: suspension, dormancy, limbo.

gre.s: Plans for the new stadium were held in ____ while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review, though officials insisted the project had not been abandoned.
gre.clue: while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review

en: Existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; not concrete
hook: ABSTRACT: pulled away (abs-tract) from the physical world.
story: Abstract. In philosophy class, Rafi's teacher asked, 'What is justice?' Rafi pointed out of the window at the court building. 'That is a building,' the teacher said. 'I asked about justice itself.' Justice, freedom and beauty are abstract: existing as ideas rather than physical things. You cannot touch them or put them in a bag. The opposite is concrete. Abstract art shows shapes and colours rather than recognizable objects. Synonyms: theoretical, conceptual, intangible.

gre.s: The professor's lectures were so ____ that students begged for concrete examples, unable to connect her elegant theories to anything in the real world.
gre.clue: students begged for concrete examples

en: An open insult; to insult intentionally
hook: AFFRONT: an insult right to your FRONT, to your face.
story: Affront. At a family wedding, Tanvir's elderly uncle was seated at the very back, behind the cooks, while younger relatives sat at the head table. He took it as a deliberate insult and left before dinner was served. He called it an affront: an open, intentional insult. As a verb, to affront someone is to insult them openly. The root means to the face, so an affront is an insult thrown right in your face. Synonyms: insult, slight, outrage.

gre.s: The ambassador regarded the decision to seat him behind junior officials as a deliberate ____, a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology.
gre.clue: a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology

en: To make someone troubled or nervous; to campaign to arouse public concern
hook: AGITATE: like a washing machine's AGITATOR, stirring things up.
story: Agitate. For years, garment workers in Savar earned wages too low to live on. Then a group of young workers began to agitate for change. They organised rallies, wrote to newspapers, and spoke at the factory gates every morning until the minimum wage was raised. To agitate is to campaign to arouse public concern. It also means to make someone troubled or nervous. Literally, it means to stir, as a washing machine agitates clothes. Synonyms: campaign, stir, unsettle.

gre.s: The doctor warned visitors not to ____ the patient with distressing news, since even mild anxiety might strain her weakened heart.
gre.clue: since even mild anxiety might strain her weakened heart

en: Respected and impressive; majestic
hook: GRE trick: au-GUST, like Emperor AUGUSTUS, majestic.
story: August. When the eighty-year-old chief justice entered the hall in his black robes, white-haired and upright, every lawyer rose in silence. Even the noisiest journalists lowered their voices. His presence was august: respected and impressive, majestic. Note the stress, aw-GUST, unlike the month. Both come from Augustus, the Roman emperor whose title meant venerable. An august institution, like an ancient university, inspires awe. Synonyms: venerable, dignified, stately.

gre.s: The young scholar felt intimidated in the ____ company of Nobel laureates and former heads of state, and barely dared to speak during the entire dinner.
gre.clue: Nobel laureates and former heads of state

en: To polish until shiny; to enhance a reputation
hook: BURNISH: rub until it BURNS bright.
story: Burnish. Every Friday, Grandfather Rahim takes out the old brass lamp his father brought from Murshidabad and rubs it with a soft cloth until it gleams like gold. He burnishes it: polishes it until it shines. Burnish is also used figuratively. A politician who donates to hospitals just before an election is trying to burnish his image, to make his reputation look brighter. Think of rubbing until the metal almost burns with light. Synonyms: polish, shine, enhance.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ her reputation after the scandal, the executive donated generously to local charities and gave interviews emphasizing her humble origins.
gre.clue: donated generously to local charities

en: Pretending to be shy; reluctant to give details
hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
story: Coy. When Nadia's friends asked whether she was engaged, she smiled, looked at the floor, and said, 'Maybe, maybe not,' while her cheeks turned pink. She clearly wanted them to keep guessing. She was being coy: pretending to be shy, or reluctant to give details. A company can also be coy about its profits, refusing to give exact numbers. Coy comes from the same Latin root as quiet. Synonyms: evasive, reticent, demure.

gre.s: The minister was uncharacteristically ____ about her plans, deflecting every question about the coming election with a smile and a vague remark about the weather.
gre.clue: deflecting every question

en: To express disapproval of; to belittle
hook: DEPRECATE: like DEPRECIATE, lowering something's value.
story: Deprecate. When Lamia won the national science fair, she told reporters, 'Oh, it was nothing, I was just lucky.' Her teachers noticed she always did this, belittling her own work. That habit is called being self-deprecating. To deprecate is to express disapproval of something, or to belittle it. Many editors deprecate the use of cliches. Do not confuse it with depreciate, which means to lose value, though the two are often mixed up. Synonyms: disparage, belittle, criticize.

gre.s: Although many modern linguists ____ strict grammar rules as elitist and arbitrary, most teachers still insist on them in student essays.
gre.clue: as elitist and arbitrary

en: The feeling that something is unworthy of respect; to scorn
hook: DIS-DAIN: you won't DEIGN to look at it.
story: Disdain. At a fancy restaurant in Banani, a wealthy man glanced at the menu, then at the waiter, and said, 'I do not eat this cheap food.' He pushed the plate away with two fingers as if it were dirty. His face showed disdain: the feeling that something is unworthy of respect. As a verb, to disdain is to scorn, so a proud person may disdain to answer a rude question. Dis means not, and the root means worthy. Synonyms: contempt, scorn.

gre.s: The aristocrat made no effort to hide his ____ for the newly rich merchants, refusing their invitations and mocking their manners at every opportunity.
gre.clue: mocking their manners at every opportunity

en: To scatter or spread over a wide area
hook: DIS-PERSE: like a SPRAY spreading out.
story: Disperse. Thousands of people gathered at Shahbag for an evening rally. When a sudden thunderstorm broke, they ran in every direction: under shop awnings, into rickshaws, down side streets. Within ten minutes the square was empty. The crowd had dispersed: scattered over a wide area. Wind disperses seeds, and police may disperse a crowd. Di means apart, and the root means to scatter. Opposite: gather, assemble. Synonyms: scatter, dissipate.

gre.s: Once the morning fog began to ____, the hikers could see the trail clearly again, though only an hour earlier the valley had been completely hidden.
gre.clue: the hikers could see the trail clearly again

en: To swell out from internal pressure
hook: DIS-TEND: EXTEND outward, swelling.
story: Distend. In photographs of famine, children often appear with thin arms but swollen bellies. Doctors explain that severe malnutrition lets fluid build up in the body, so the stomach becomes distended: swollen out from internal pressure. To distend is to swell from within. A balloon distends as you blow air into it. Dis means apart, and tend means stretch, so distend means stretched apart. Do not confuse it with distort. Synonyms: swell, bloat, inflate.

gre.s: After swallowing its prey whole, the python's body began to ____ visibly, its skin stretching to accommodate an animal nearly twice its own width.
gre.clue: its skin stretching to accommodate

en: Native to or regularly found in a particular place or group
hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
story: Endemic. Every monsoon, dengue fever returns to Dhaka. Doctors no longer treat it as a surprise; it is always present, rising and falling with the rains. Dengue is endemic in Bangladesh: regularly found in that place. The word also describes plants and animals native to one area, like the lemurs found only on Madagascar. Contrast it with epidemic, a sudden outbreak. En means in, and demos means people. Synonyms: native, prevalent, entrenched.

gre.s: Corruption was so ____ in the old regime that bribery was considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal.
gre.clue: considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal

en: Deep hostility; the state of being enemies
hook: ENMITY: ENEMY-ity.
story: Enmity. Two rival shopkeepers in Old Dhaka have not spoken for twenty years. They were once partners, until one accused the other of stealing. Now they cut prices just to hurt each other, warn customers against each other, and even their sons fight in the street. Between them lies deep enmity: hostility, the state of being enemies. Enmity and enemy share a root. Its opposite is amity, which means friendship. Synonyms: hostility, animosity, antagonism.

gre.s: The ____ between the two clans, rooted in a dispute over land generations earlier, was so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings.
gre.clue: so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings

en: Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact
hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
story: Gauche. At his first office party, Farhan asked his boss's wife how old she was, laughed loudly at the wrong moment, and wiped his hands on the tablecloth. Everyone smiled politely and looked away. His behaviour was gauche: socially awkward, lacking grace or tact. Gauche is French for left, from an old prejudice that the left hand is clumsy. Its opposite, adroit, comes from the French for right. Synonyms: awkward, tactless, maladroit.

gre.s: Though brilliant in the laboratory, the young chemist was painfully ____ at receptions, blurting out tactless remarks and forgetting the names of her hosts.
gre.clue: blurting out tactless remarks

en: Showing uncontrolled emotion; extremely funny
hook: HYSTERICAL: emotions out of control, crying or laughing.
story: Hysterical. When the lights went out during a thunderstorm, Mitu's little cousin began screaming, crying and running around the room, and nobody could calm her for half an hour. She was hysterical: showing uncontrolled emotion. Strangely, the same word has a happy sense too. The next day, their uncle told a story so funny that the whole family laughed until they cried. Everyone agreed it was hysterical: extremely funny. Synonyms: frantic, overwrought, and for humour, hilarious.

gre.s: News of the crash reached the families before any official statement, and the airport lounge became a scene of ____ grief, with relatives sobbing and screaming uncontrollably.
gre.clue: sobbing and screaming uncontrollably

en: Shamelessly rude and disrespectful
hook: IM-PUDENT: no shame (pudor = shame).
story: Impudent. When Mahin's younger brother was told to finish his homework, he stuck out his tongue at their father, said, 'Do it yourself,' and walked away whistling. Their father was too shocked to speak. The boy's reply was impudent: shamelessly rude and disrespectful. Impudent comes from the Latin for without shame, the opposite of pudor, meaning modesty. Impudent and insolent are near twins. Synonyms: cheeky, impertinent, brazen.

gre.s: The ____ student not only ignored the teacher's warning but mimicked her voice in front of the whole class, apparently without the slightest shame.
gre.clue: apparently without the slightest shame

en: Just begun and not fully formed
hook: INCHOATE: like a chick just INCHing out of its egg, not yet formed.
story: Inchoate. At two in the morning, Ishita had half an idea for a startup, something about connecting village farmers directly with city buyers. She scribbled a few words, drew some arrows, and fell asleep. The plan was inchoate: just begun and not fully formed. Say it in-KOH-it. It comes from the Latin for beginning, and despite the sound, it has nothing to do with chaos. An inchoate feeling is one you cannot yet put into words. Synonyms: embryonic, rudimentary, nascent.

gre.s: The committee's proposals remained ____, little more than a list of vague goals that had yet to be developed into any concrete plan.
gre.clue: had yet to be developed into any concrete plan

en: A strong liking or habitual tendency
hook: PENCHANT: leaning toward it like a PENDANT hangs down.
story: Penchant. Arif cannot pass a roadside tea stall without stopping. He drinks six cups a day, knows the best stall in every neighbourhood, and plans his walks around them. He has a penchant for tea: a strong liking or habitual tendency. Penchant comes from the French for leaning, so a penchant is something you lean toward. One may also have a penchant for exaggeration or for arriving late. Synonyms: fondness, inclination, proclivity.

gre.s: Given the senator's well-known ____ for theatrical gestures, no one was surprised when he tore up the bill on live television.
gre.clue: no one was surprised

en: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
hook: QUANDARY: 'QUAND?' (when?) and 'where?' — totally stuck.
story: Quandary. Two job offers reached Nadia on the same day. One was in Dhaka, close to her ailing mother, with a modest salary. The other was in Singapore, with double the pay and a real chance to build a career. She paced the hostel corridor all night, unable to decide. She was in a quandary: a state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation. A quandary is close to a dilemma. Synonyms: dilemma, predicament, plight.

gre.s: The doctor faced a genuine ____: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate her duty of honesty.
gre.clue: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate

en: Isolation to prevent the spread of disease; to isolate
hook: QUARANTINE: from Italian 'quaranta', forty days of isolation for ships.
story: Quarantine. In the spring of 2020, Zayan returned from abroad just as the pandemic was spreading. At the airport, officials sent him to a hotel room for fourteen days. He could not visit his family or even step into the corridor. That period of isolation was a quarantine: isolation to prevent the spread of disease. As a verb, to quarantine is to isolate. The word comes from the Italian for forty days, the time ships once waited outside Venice.

gre.s: Health officials decided to ____ the entire village after the outbreak, barring anyone from leaving until tests confirmed that the virus was no longer spreading.
gre.clue: barring anyone from leaving

en: To forcefully stop or suppress; to officially reject
hook: QUASH: SQUASH it flat.
story: Quash. A student newspaper at Sara's university uncovered a cheating scandal involving the son of a wealthy donor. Within hours, the administration ordered the article removed and threatened the editors. They were trying to quash the story: to forcefully stop or suppress it. In law, to quash means to officially reject, as when a higher court quashes a conviction. Think of squash, crushing something flat. Synonyms: suppress, crush, annul.

gre.s: The regime moved swiftly to ____ the rebellion, arresting its leaders and banning public gatherings before the unrest could spread to other cities.
gre.clue: before the unrest could spread to other cities

en: To argue about trivial matters; a minor objection
hook: QUIBBLE: a small QUIBBLE, like a QUIBBLING nibble.
story: Quibble. Shuvo and his roommate argued for twenty minutes about whether they had bought five eggs or six, and whether the electricity bill was two hundred and ten taka or two hundred and twelve. Meanwhile, their dinner burned on the stove. They were quibbling: arguing about trivial matters. A quibble is also a minor objection, as in, my only quibble with the book is its tiny font. Synonyms: nitpick, cavil, carp.

gre.s: The reviewer admired the novel's ambition and its vivid characters; her only ____ concerned a handful of typographical errors that hardly diminished its power.
gre.clue: that hardly diminished its power

en: To cause severe and extensive damage
hook: RAVAGE: like a RAVENOUS SAVAGE destroying everything.
story: Ravage. In 2007, Cyclone Sidr struck the southwest coast of Bangladesh. Winds tore roofs from houses, the storm surge swept away fields and livestock, and whole villages were flattened. Cyclones like this ravage the coast: they cause severe and extensive damage. The ravages of time, war or disease are their destructive effects. Do not confuse ravage with ravish, which means to seize or enrapture. Synonyms: devastate, destroy, wreck.

gre.s: Unless farmers act quickly to control the locusts, the swarms will ____ the region's crops, leaving little to harvest and threatening famine.
gre.clue: leaving little to harvest

en: To publicly withdraw a statement or belief
hook: RE-CANT: un-CHANT what you said.
story: Recant. In 1633, the astronomer Galileo was brought before the Church and forced, under threat of punishment, to declare that the Earth does not move around the sun. He publicly recanted: he withdrew his statement and belief. Legend says he whispered afterwards, 'And yet it moves.' Re means back, and cant comes from the Latin for sing, so to recant is to sing your words back. Synonyms: retract, renounce, disavow.

gre.s: Despite intense pressure from church authorities, the scientist refused to ____ his theory, insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming.
gre.clue: insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming

en: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
story: Redoubtable. In the chess club at Joya's school, one quiet girl had not lost a game in three years. Seniors avoided playing her, and visiting champions left shaking their heads. She was redoubtable: formidable, especially as an opponent, and worthy of respect. It comes from the Old French redouter, to dread, so a redoubtable person is someone others dread to face. Sports writers love it for a fierce rival team. Synonyms: formidable, fearsome, impressive.

gre.s: Even seasoned lawyers dreaded facing her in court, for she was a ____ advocate whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses.
gre.clue: whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses

en: Shy and tending to avoid company
hook: GRE trick: RETIRING means shy — she RETIRES to her room when guests come.
story: Retiring. At every family gathering, Priya's cousin Sabbir sits quietly in a corner with a book. He smiles when spoken to but never starts a conversation, and he slips away before the group photographs. He is retiring: shy and tending to avoid company. This has nothing to do with stopping work at sixty, though both involve withdrawing. A retiring person withdraws from attention. Synonyms: reserved, diffident, shy.

gre.s: Though her paintings were bold and flamboyant, the artist herself was ____, avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions.
gre.clue: avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions

en: High-pitched and piercing; loud and forceful in criticism
hook: SHRILL: like a SHRIEKING whistle.
story: Shrill. In Babu's flat, the pressure cooker whistle pierced the air, and a moment later his little sister shrieked at the cat. Both sounds were shrill: high-pitched and piercing. Shrill also describes criticism that is loud and forceful, often too forceful. One newspaper attacked the minister in shrill editorials every single day, until readers stopped listening. Say the word aloud and you can hear its sharp, whistling sound. Synonyms: piercing, strident.

gre.s: The opposition's attacks grew increasingly ____, so loud and relentless that even sympathetic voters began to dismiss them as hysteria rather than reasoned argument.
gre.clue: so loud and relentless

en: Clever but deliberately misleading argument
hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
story: Sophistry. Caught looking at notes during an exam, Imran argued that he had not cheated, because the answers were already in his memory and the notes merely reminded him. For a moment it sounded clever, but it was nonsense. His argument was sophistry: clever but deliberately misleading reasoning. The Sophists were ancient Greek teachers accused of training students to win arguments rather than find the truth. Synonyms: casuistry, specious reasoning.

gre.s: The lawyer's defense, though dazzlingly clever, was mere ____: each step seemed logical, yet the argument as a whole was designed to mislead the jury.
gre.clue: designed to mislead the jury

en: To provide evidence to support or prove
hook: SUBSTANTIATE: give it SUBSTANCE.
story: Substantiate. Rumana claimed that a factory upstream was poisoning the river. Officials laughed: 'Where is your proof?' So she collected water samples every week, had them tested in a university lab, and photographed the dead fish. Her report substantiated the claim: it provided evidence that supported it. The factory was fined. To substantiate is to give substance to a claim. Its opposite is refute. Synonyms: corroborate, verify, prove.

gre.s: The reporter's allegations, however sensational, were dismissed because she could not ____ them with any documents or credible witnesses.
gre.clue: with any documents or credible witnesses

en: Skilled at gaining advantage through cunning
hook: WILY: like WILE E. Coyote, always scheming.
story: Wily. In a famous Bengali folk tale, a crocodile sends her seven babies to the jackal to be educated. Each day the jackal eats one. Whenever the mother visits, he holds up the same surviving baby again and again, and she leaves happy. The jackal is wily: skilled at gaining advantage through cunning. Wily comes from wile, a clever trick. Contrast it with guileless, which means innocent and open. Synonyms: cunning, crafty, sly.

gre.s: The ____ negotiator let her opponents believe they had won every minor point, all the while maneuvering toward the one concession she actually wanted.
gre.clue: all the while maneuvering toward
